title: 1. Set up the environment
text: Set up the R environment used in the tutorial, either via the workshop cloud environment or locally on your laptop.

title: 1. Set up the environment
text:
Option A (recommended): Workshop RStudio environment
Note: This option was only available during the workshop. Otherwise, use Option B.
A virtual machine running RStudio Server is available in PDC Cloud. Log in using the credentials provided during the workshop:
RStudio Server (available during workshop only)
Follow the tutorial steps and avoid creating additional large objects, as resources are shared. Save your work regularly as an R script. The virtual machine will be shut down after the workshop, so download any code or output you want to keep via the Files pane (More → Export).

Check required packages
All required packages are pre-installed in the workshop environment. Load them and confirm that they are available:
library(asvoccur)
library(ranger)
library(vegan)
library(ape)
library(rworldmap)
library(lubridate)
library(data.table)


Check access to example data
For this tutorial, ASV portal data is pre-downloaded and available on the virtual machine. Check access:
data_path <- "/srv/course-data/COI"
list.files(data_path)
If two COI zip files are listed, you are ready to proceed.

section: Option B (fallback): Run RStudio locally on your laptop
text:
Option B (fallback): Run RStudio locally on your laptop
You will need to install:

R
RStudio
the following R packages:

remotes
asvoccur
ranger
vegan
ape

lubridate

To install and load the required R packages:
# Install from CRAN
install.packages(c(
  "remotes",
  "ranger",
  "vegan",
  "ape",
  "rworldmap",
  "lubridate",
  "data.table"
))

# Install from GitHub
remotes::install_github("biodiversitydata-se/asvoccur")

# Load
library(asvoccur)
library(ranger)
library(vegan)
library(ape)
library(rworldmap)
library(lubridate)
library(data.table)

# Confirm version
packageVersion("asvoccur")  # Should say 1.1.1

Download example data from the ASV portal
In this option, example data is downloaded directly from the ASV portal.

Go to the ASV portal start page.
Click DOWNLOAD. If you are not already logged in, you will be redirected to the login page.
If you do not already have an account, either:

sign in with a Google or GitHub account, or
create a new SBDI account.

On the Download page, under Download link, download the following datasets:

IBA_CO1_homogenate_2019_SE
IBA_CO1_soil_litter_2019_SE

After downloading, place both zip files in a single folder:
course-data/
└── COI/
    ├── IBA_CO1_homogenate_2019_SE.zip
    └── IBA_CO1_soil_litter_2019_SE.zip
Set the path to the data folder in R and confirm access:

data_path <- "local/path/to/course-data/COI"
list.files(data_path)
If both zip files are listed, you are ready to proceed.

title: 2. Prepare data
text:
Load, merge and aggregate ASV portal data into a format suitable for downstream analyses.

Load the datasets
Load the two COI datasets using the data_path object defined in the previous section:
loaded <- load_data(data_path)
This reads datasets into the loaded object, which you can inspect using the magnifying glass next to it in the Environment pane. The object is a list organised into data type sub-lists, each containing one table or matrix element per dataset:

counts: ASV read counts
asvs: ASV sequences and taxonomic annotations
events: core sample-level metadata (where, when, how, who)
datasets: dataset-level metadata
emof: dataset-specific extended measurement or fact contextual data

Sparse matrices (dgCMatrix) are used to reduce memory usage for count data, while tabular structures (data.table) are used for metadata. To see dataset sizes, inspect the elements in counts, where sizes are shown as matrix dimensions (e.g. IBA_CO1_ethanol_2019_SE: dgCMatrix [X x 200], corresponding to the number of ASVs × samples).
To see the full function documentation for load_data:
?asvoccur::load_data



Merge the datasets
The two datasets share the same 200 sampling sites but use different collection methods: Malaise traps catch flying and actively moving insects, while soil/litter extraction targets ground-dwelling invertebrates. We merge them to analyse both together:
merged <- merge_data(loaded)
The merged object is a list with one combined object per data type (counts, events, asvs, datasets, emof), represented as a sparse matrix for count data and data tables for metadata, as in loaded.



Convert merged metadata to data frames
Convert the metadata tables to data frame format for convenience. The count matrix (merged$counts) is kept as a sparse matrix and used directly in downstream analyses — converting it to a dense data frame would be very memory-intensive for large datasets:
merged_df <- convert_to_df(merged)
To inspect the sample names:
colnames(merged$counts)
ASVs shared across datasets are merged using SBDI ASV IDs. These IDs correspond to MD5 hashes of the sequences, meaning that ASVs with identical sequences are represented only once.



Aggregate counts by taxonomy
We now aggregate ASV read counts at different taxonomic levels based on the taxonomic annotation:
cladecounts <- sum_by_clade(merged$counts, merged$asvs)
This produces aggregated counts at the following levels:

kingdom (or domain)
phylum
class
order
family
genus
species
otu (if available)

We convert the result to data frame format:
cladecounts_df <- convert_to_df(cladecounts)
Both raw counts and normalised counts (relative abundances per sample) are available. For example:
cladecounts_df$raw$phylum[1:3, 1:3]  # raw counts at phylum level
cladecounts_df$norm$order[1:3, 1:3]  # relative abundances at order level
At this point, the data are ready for exploration and analysis.

title: Exploring eDNA in SBDI
text: Welcome to the Exploring eDNA in SBDI workshop at BioSyst EU 2026, Uppsala, 17–19 August 2026!

title: Exploring eDNA in SBDI
text:
Description
This workshop will demonstrate how environmental DNA (eDNA) / metabarcoding data can be accessed, processed, and analysed within the Swedish Biodiversity Data Infrastructure (SBDI). We will show how to download eDNA data, use our R package to unpack, merge, and aggregate datasets, and then explore arthropod biodiversity patterns across habitat types in Sweden using COI metabarcoding data from the Insect Biome Atlas. The session will also introduce SBDI resources for data submission, processing, and integration with GBIF.

title: Exploring eDNA in SBDI
text:
Expected outcomes
Participants will learn about tools and workflows for eDNA data management and analysis, and how these contribute to open biodiversity knowledge.

title: Exploring eDNA in SBDI
text:
Instructors

Dr. Maria Prager — SBDI & University of Gothenburg

title: 7. Air vs. ground communities
text:
Compare arthropod communities from Malaise traps (flying insects) and soil/litter extraction (ground-dwelling invertebrates) using genus-level Bray–Curtis distances.
Because the two sampling methods target different ecological layers, we expect their communities to differ systematically — regardless of habitat. Here we test that expectation and identify which taxonomic groups drive the difference.

Bray–Curtis distances on genus composition
We use genus-level normalised counts rather than ASV-level counts. This reduces the effect of sequencing noise and makes the comparison more robust across sampling methods:
bray_dist <- as.matrix(vegdist(t(cladecounts_df$norm$genus), method = "bray"))


Run PCoA
pcoa_res2 <- pcoa(bray_dist, correction = "cailliez")


Plot PCoA (genus level)
Point shape distinguishes sampling method; point colour shows habitat type as before.
layout(matrix(c(1, 2, 3, 3), 2, 2, byrow = TRUE))
par(mar = c(5, 5, 2, 1), xpd = TRUE, cex.axis = 1)

xlab <- paste0("PC1 (", round(pcoa_res2$values$Rel_corr_eig[1] * 100), "%)")
ylab <- paste0("PC2 (", round(pcoa_res2$values$Rel_corr_eig[2] * 100), "%)")

# Panel: Malaise trap
plot(pcoa_res2$vectors[, 1], pcoa_res2$vectors[, 2],
     pch = pch, col = "white", bg = "white",
     xlab = xlab, ylab = ylab, main = "Malaise trap")
points(pcoa_res2$vectors[DS_malaise, 1], pcoa_res2$vectors[DS_malaise, 2],
       pch = pch[DS_malaise], col = "black",
       bg  = color_habitat[DS_malaise], cex = 1.4)

# Panel: Soil/litter
plot(pcoa_res2$vectors[, 1], pcoa_res2$vectors[, 2],
     pch = pch, col = "white", bg = "white",
     xlab = xlab, ylab = ylab, main = "Soil/litter")
points(pcoa_res2$vectors[DS_soillitter, 1], pcoa_res2$vectors[DS_soillitter, 2],
       pch = pch[DS_soillitter], col = "black",
       bg  = color_habitat[DS_soillitter], cex = 1.4)

# Legend
plot.new()
legend("center", bty = "n",
       legend = names(habitat_cols),
       pt.bg  = habitat_cols,
       pch = 21, pt.cex = 1.6, cex = 1.1,
       title = "Habitat")


Which orders differ between methods?
We plot the mean relative abundance of insect orders in each sampling method to see which taxonomic groups are over-represented in the air vs. the ground layer:
orders <- rownames(cladecounts_df$norm$order)

mean_malaise    <- rowMeans(cladecounts_df$norm$order[, DS_malaise,    drop = FALSE])
mean_soillitter <- rowMeans(cladecounts_df$norm$order[, DS_soillitter, drop = FALSE])

top <- order(pmax(mean_malaise, mean_soillitter), decreasing = TRUE)[1:10]

par(mfrow = c(1, 1), mar = c(5, 10, 2, 2))
barplot(
  rbind(mean_malaise[top], mean_soillitter[top]),
  beside  = TRUE,
  horiz   = TRUE,
  names.arg = orders[top],
  col     = c("#4895ef", "#d4a017"),
  las     = 1,
  xlab    = "Mean relative abundance",
  main    = "Top orders by sampling method"
)
legend("bottomright", bty = "n",
       legend = c("Malaise trap", "Soil/litter"),
       fill   = c("#4895ef", "#d4a017"))

title: Import and analyse ASV portal data with R
text:
This tutorial walks through the main steps needed to integrate ASV portal data in R and explore biodiversity patterns. As a case study, we use COI metabarcoding data from the Insect Biome Atlas (IBA) project to examine arthropod community composition across habitat types in Sweden.
In 2019, the IBA project collected arthropod samples at 200 sites spanning six habitat types — forest, cropland, wetland, grassland, urban and alpine. The full Swedish IBA dataset comprises four COI datasets that differ in both sampling method (Malaise trap vs. soil/litter extraction) and DNA extraction protocol (ethanol preservation, homogenate, or lysate). Here we use two of those datasets: a Malaise trap homogenate dataset (862 samples, ~142 000 ASVs) and a soil/litter dataset (348 samples, ~31 000 ASVs). Both use the same COI primers, making ASVs directly comparable across methods. Together they capture differences both across habitat types and between the air and ground layers of the ecosystem.
Sections 1–6 work with both datasets combined, using habitat type as the main explanatory variable. Section 7 zooms in on the contrast between the two sampling methods.

Set up the environment — Access the workshop RStudio environment (or run locally)
Prepare data — Load, merge and aggregate data sourced from the ASV portal
Map samples — Explore sampling coverage across Sweden and habitat types
Community structure — Bray–Curtis distances and PCoA across samples
Taxonomic composition — Taxonomic barplots across habitat types
Predict habitat type (Random Forest) — Random Forest classification from community composition
Air vs. ground communities — Genus-level comparison between Malaise trap and soil/litter samples

Get started →

Reference
Miraldo, A., Sundh, J., Iwaszkiewicz-Eggebrecht, E., Buczek, M., Goodsell, R., Johansson, H., Fisher, B. L., Raharinjanahary, D., Rajoelison, E. T., Ranaivo, C., Randrianandrasana, C., Rafanomezantsoa, J.-J., Manoharan, L., Granqvist, E., van Dijk, L. J. A., Alberg, L., Åhlén, D., Aspebo, M., Åström, S., … Ronquist, F. (2025). Data of the Insect Biome Atlas: A metabarcoding survey of the terrestrial arthropods of Sweden and Madagascar. Scientific Data, 12(1), 1–18.

title: 3. Map samples
text:
Explore the spatial distribution of samples and their associated habitat types across Sweden.

Inspect contextual data
Core sample-level metadata is available in merged_df$events:
colnames(merged_df$events)
Samples are ordered consistently across tables, which makes it straightforward to link sequence data with contextual data. Thus, rownames(merged_df$events), rownames(merged_df$emof) and colnames(merged$counts) refer to the same samples.
To identify samples from each dataset:
DS_malaise    <- grep("homogenate", rownames(merged_df$events))
DS_soillitter <- grep("soil_litter", rownames(merged_df$events))



Extract spatial and temporal variables
lat   <- merged_df$events$decimalLatitude
lon   <- merged_df$events$decimalLongitude
month <- lubridate::month(merged_df$events$eventDate)
yday  <- lubridate::yday(merged_df$events$eventDate)



Extract habitat type
The env_local_scale column contains habitat type classifications based on the Environment Ontology (ENVO). We first inspect the unique values:
unique(merged_df$events$env_local_scale)
For plotting, we create short labels and assign a colour to each habitat:
habitat_map <- c(
  "ENVO:00000091" = "forest",
  "ENVO:00000077" = "cropland",
  "ENVO:00000043" = "wetland",
  "ENVO:00000054" = "grassland",
  "ENVO:01000249" = "urban",
  "ENVO:00000213" = "alpine"
)
habitat <- habitat_map[merged_df$events$env_local_scale]

habitat_cols <- c(
  "forest"    = "#2d6a4f",
  "cropland"  = "#d4a017",
  "wetland"   = "#4895ef",
  "grassland" = "#95d5b2",
  "urban"     = "#adb5bd",
  "alpine"    = "#9b5de5"
)
color_habitat <- habitat_cols[habitat]






Note



Note: Check the output of unique(merged_df$events$env_local_scale) and adjust the habitat_map vector if the ENVO identifiers differ from those shown above.





Prepare plotting symbols
We define sampling-method-specific plotting symbols:
pch <- rep(NA, nrow(merged_df$events))
pch[DS_malaise]    <- 21  # circle: Malaise trap
pch[DS_soillitter] <- 22  # square: soil/litter



Map samples
We plot all sites on a map of Sweden, with point colour indicating habitat type and point shape indicating sampling method:
newmap <- rworldmap::getMap(resolution = "low")

par(mar = c(2, 2, 2, 2))
plot(newmap,
     xlim = c(10, 25),
     ylim = c(55, 70),
     asp  = 1,
     main = "IBA sampling sites")

points(lon, lat,
       col = "black",
       bg  = color_habitat,
       pch = pch,
       cex = 1.2)

legend("bottomleft", bty = "n",
       legend = names(habitat_cols),
       pt.bg  = habitat_cols,
       pch    = 21, pt.cex = 1.4, cex = 0.9,
       title  = "Habitat")

legend("bottomright", bty = "n",
       legend = c("Malaise trap", "Soil/litter"),
       pch    = c(21, 22), pt.cex = 1.4, cex = 0.9,
       title  = "Method")

title: 6. Classify habitat type (Random Forest)
text:
Use Random Forest to classify habitat type from community composition data.
Here we train a classifier that predicts the habitat type of a sample from its arthropod community composition. Good classification accuracy suggests that the community composition is a reliable indicator of habitat.

Choose target variable
We use habitat type as the target:
y <- as.factor(habitat)
Remove samples with missing habitat labels:
ok <- which(!is.na(y))
y  <- y[ok]


Create a feature matrix
We use relative abundances of ASVs as features (norm_sparse created in 4). By filtering rare ASVs in sparse space before converting to dense, we avoid creating a large intermediate matrix:
X_sparse <- Matrix::t(norm_sparse)[ok, , drop = FALSE]  # samples × ASVs (sparse)

# Filter ASVs present in <10% of samples
keep <- which(Matrix::colSums(X_sparse > 0) / nrow(X_sparse) >= 0.1)

# Convert to dense only after filtering
X <- as.matrix(X_sparse[, keep, drop = FALSE])


Train/test split
Split the data into training and test sets to evaluate model performance on unseen samples.
set.seed(1)
n         <- nrow(X)
train_ix  <- sample(seq_len(n), size = round(0.8 * n))
test_ix   <- setdiff(seq_len(n), train_ix)

X_train <- X[train_ix, , drop = FALSE]
y_train <- y[train_ix]

X_test  <- X[test_ix, , drop = FALSE]
y_test  <- y[test_ix]


Train Random Forest
We train a random forest classifier using the R package ranger.
rf <- ranger(
  x          = X_train,
  y          = y_train,
  num.trees  = 500,
  importance = "permutation"
)
500 trees gives a good balance between accuracy and runtime for tutorial datasets. For production models, increasing to 1000–5000 trees can improve stability.


Predict and evaluate
Assess model performance by predicting habitat type for the test data.
pred <- predict(rf, data = X_test)$predictions

# Overall accuracy
mean(pred == y_test)

# Confusion matrix
table(Predicted = pred, Observed = y_test)
A confusion matrix shows which habitat types are correctly classified and which are confused with each other. High off-diagonal values for a pair of habitats suggest their arthropod communities are similar.


Variable importance (optional)
Identify which ASVs contribute most to habitat classification.
imp <- sort(rf$variable.importance, decreasing = TRUE)
plot(imp, xlab = "ASV rank", ylab = "Permutation importance")
To get the taxonomy of the 10 most important ASVs:
merged_df$asvs[names(imp[1:10]), 7:10]

title: 4. Community structure (PCoA)
text:
Analyse community composition using Bray–Curtis distances and visualise patterns with a Principal Coordinates Analysis (PCoA).

Normalise counts to relative abundances
First, convert ASV counts to relative abundances per sample. Normalising in sparse space avoids creating a large dense intermediate matrix:
col_totals <- Matrix::colSums(merged$counts)
norm_sparse <- Matrix::t(Matrix::t(merged$counts) / col_totals)
norm_counts <- as.matrix(norm_sparse)
norm_sparse retains the sparse structure and is reused in 6. norm_counts is the dense version required by vegdist.


Calculate Bray–Curtis distances
Compute pairwise Bray–Curtis distances (beta-diversity):
bray_dist <- as.matrix(vegdist(t(norm_counts), method = "bray"))






Note



Scaling to larger datasets. The dense matrix norm_counts (ASVs × samples) and the n×n distance matrix can become large. Two recommended steps before this point when working with many ASVs or samples:

Filter rare ASVs to reduce norm_counts before the as.matrix() call — e.g. keep only ASVs present in ≥5% of samples:
keep_asvs <- which(Matrix::rowSums(norm_sparse > 0) / ncol(norm_sparse) >= 0.05)
norm_counts <- as.matrix(norm_sparse[keep_asvs, ])
Subsample samples if n > ~1 000: pcoa() performs a full eigendecomposition (O(n³)), which becomes slow above a few thousand samples.





Run PCoA
Perform Principal Coordinates Analysis on the distance matrix:
pcoa_res <- pcoa(bray_dist, correction = "cailliez")


Plot PCoA results
We plot samples in PCoA space using the first two axes. Point colour shows habitat type; point shape shows sampling method. Two panels separate the two datasets for clarity.
layout(matrix(c(1, 2, 3, 3), 2, 2, byrow = TRUE))
par(mar = c(5, 5, 2, 1), xpd = TRUE, cex.axis = 1)

xlab <- paste0("PC1 (", round(pcoa_res$values$Rel_corr_eig[1] * 100), "%)")
ylab <- paste0("PC2 (", round(pcoa_res$values$Rel_corr_eig[2] * 100), "%)")

# Panel: Malaise trap
plot(pcoa_res$vectors[, 1], pcoa_res$vectors[, 2],
     pch = pch, col = "white", bg = "white",
     xlab = xlab, ylab = ylab, main = "Malaise trap")
points(pcoa_res$vectors[DS_malaise, 1], pcoa_res$vectors[DS_malaise, 2],
       pch = pch[DS_malaise], col = "black",
       bg  = color_habitat[DS_malaise],
       cex = 1.4)

# Panel: Soil/litter
plot(pcoa_res$vectors[, 1], pcoa_res$vectors[, 2],
     pch = pch, col = "white", bg = "white",
     xlab = xlab, ylab = ylab, main = "Soil/litter")
points(pcoa_res$vectors[DS_soillitter, 1], pcoa_res$vectors[DS_soillitter, 2],
       pch = pch[DS_soillitter], col = "black",
       bg  = color_habitat[DS_soillitter],
       cex = 1.4)

# Legend
plot.new()
legend("center", bty = "n",
       legend = names(habitat_cols),
       pt.bg  = habitat_cols,
       pch    = 21, pt.cex = 1.6, cex = 1.1,
       title  = "Habitat")
Interpretation: the PCoA shows whether community composition is structured by habitat type, sampling method, or both.

title: 5. Taxonomic composition and barplots
text:
Summarise taxonomic composition across habitat types and seasons using stacked barplots.

Define the barplot function
The function below aggregates monthly averages within each habitat type and plots stacked barplots for the top taxa.
plot_barplots <- function(rank, size_taxa = -1, main = "", top_x = 10) {
  mycols <- colorRampPalette(c(
    "#a6cee3", "#1f78b4", "#b2df8a", "#33a02c",
    "#fb9a99", "#e31a1c", "#fdbf6f", "#ff7f00",
    "#cab2d6", "#6a3d9a", "#ffff99", "#b15928"
  ))
  habitats <- names(habitat_cols)
  par(mfrow = c(length(habitats), 1), mar = c(2, 3, 2, 14), xpd = TRUE)
  ok <- sort(rowMeans(cladecounts_df$norm[[rank]]),
             index.return = TRUE, decreasing = TRUE)$ix[1:top_x]
  if (size_taxa == -1) { size_taxa <- min(1.5, 8 / length(ok)) }
  for (hab in habitats) {
    ix <- which(habitat == hab)
    monthly_averages_matr <- matrix(ncol = 12, nrow = nrow(cladecounts_df$norm[[rank]]))
    for (j in 1:12) {
      ix2 <- intersect(ix, which(month == j))
      if (length(ix2) > 1) { monthly_averages_matr[, j] <- rowMeans(cladecounts_df$norm[[rank]][, ix2]) }
      if (length(ix2) == 1) { monthly_averages_matr[, j] <- cladecounts_df$norm[[rank]][, ix2] }
      if (length(ix2) == 0) { monthly_averages_matr[, j] <- 0 }
    }
    barplot(monthly_averages_matr[ok, ], col = mycols(length(ok)),
            main = hab)
    legend("bottomleft", bty = "n", pch = 19,
           col    = mycols(length(ok))[length(ok):1],
           cex    = size_taxa, inset = c(1, 0),
           legend = rownames(cladecounts_df$norm[[rank]])[rev(ok)])
  }
}


Note on taxonomic ranks
Use numeric rank codes where: 1 = kingdom (or domain), 2 = phylum, 3 = class, 4 = order, 5 = family, 6 = genus, 7 = species.


Example: plot top orders
Plot the 8 most abundant insect orders across habitat types:
plot_barplots(rank = 4, top_x = 8)
This creates one stacked barplot row per habitat type, each showing monthly averages for the selected taxa. You can also adjust the size of the taxa legend with the size_taxa parameter.
